opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more interesting results in this space, because on its face it shouldn't work as well as it does. You're not teaching the model any of the facts you later test it on. You're showing it some true statements and nudging it to treat them as true, and somehow that transfers to judgments about completely different propositions.

The most natural explanation, and the one I find most compelling, is that these models already have something like an internal representation of truthfulness, or at least of "what a reliable, knowledgeable speaker would assert." Pretraining data is a mixture of many speakers: people who are right, people who are wrong, people writing fiction, people joking. A model trained to predict all of that has to track, at least implicitly, which kind of speaker it's currently modeling. So a lot of the knowledge is in there, but the model doesn't consistently use it, because it's not always clear which persona it's supposed to be simulating.

Under that view, fine-tuning on true sentences isn't installing knowledge. It's selecting a mode. You're pushing the model toward the part of its distribution that corresponds to an informed, truthful agent, and once it's there, its existing knowledge about unrelated facts becomes more accessible. That's why the gains generalize: the thing being learned is not a fact but a disposition.

I'd add a couple of caveats. One is that we should be careful about what "verify" means. Improving accuracy on a true/false benchmark doesn't necessarily mean the model has a coherent belief state. A model can get better at classifying individual statements while still being inconsistent across paraphrases, or across a statement and its logical consequences. So I'd want to see whether these interventions also improve coherence, not just pointwise accuracy.

The other is that this cuts both ways. If a small amount of fine-tuning can shift the model toward a truthful persona, it can presumably shift it away from one too, and it may also shift it toward whatever narrow notion of "truth" happens to be reflected in your fine-tuning set. That matters a lot if you're thinking about this as an alignment or reliability tool.

But overall, I think it's encouraging. It suggests that a meaningful part of the hallucination and factuality problem is less about missing knowledge and more about getting models to consistently use what they already know. And that's a problem we have a reasonable chance of making progress on, both with training interventions like this and with interpretability methods that try to locate and steer those truth-related representations directly.

r001.rationale: The response says the model already has relevant knowledge and an internal representation of truthfulness, and that fine-tuning makes this existing capability more accessible for judging unrelated facts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those results that I find genuinely surprising, and I think it's worth being careful about what it does and doesn't tell us.

The setup is roughly: you take a model, you fine-tune it on a bunch of sentences that happen to be true, with no particular topical structure, and then you ask it to judge whether some completely unrelated statement is true or false. And its accuracy on that judgment task goes up. Not by a huge amount, but reliably, and in a way that doesn't happen if you fine-tune on an equal number of false sentences, or on sentences with mixed truth values.

The naive story, that the model is "learning facts," doesn't really work, because the test facts aren't in the training set. So the interesting question is what's actually changing. My read is that it's something closer to a shift in the model's default mode. Pretraining data is full of text that's false in all sorts of ways: fiction, errors, sarcasm, opinions presented as fact, old information. The model has to represent all of that, and at inference time it's partly guessing which regime it's in. When you fine-tune on text that's uniformly true, you may be nudging the model toward treating the "say true things" regime as the default, and that default then carries over to how it evaluates novel claims.

There's some evidence for this in the representation work. People have found that models seem to encode something like a truth direction, a feature that separates true from false statements fairly linearly, even across domains. I'm cautious about over-interpreting those probes, because it's hard to distinguish "truth" from things like "sounds confident" or "is the kind of sentence a textbook would contain." But if there is some shared internal variable like that, then fine-tuning on true statements could be sharpening it, or making the model attend to it more when producing judgments. That would explain the generalization to unrelated domains.

What I'd want to see before I'm fully convinced is a couple of things. One is good controls for surface features. True sentences and false sentences differ stylistically in ways that are hard to fully strip out, and you want to know that the effect survives when you match for those. Another is whether it's really about truth or about calibration. It's possible the fine-tuning is mostly making the model less willing to go along with a plausible-sounding false premise, which is useful, but is a slightly different story than "the model got better at knowing things."

From a practical standpoint, if it holds up, it's kind of a nice result. Verification is one of the places where we most want models to be reliable, and this suggests that the data you train on shapes not just what the model knows but how it reasons about epistemic status in general. It's also a bit of a warning in the other direction. If training on true sentences helps, training on a lot of low-quality or false text presumably hurts in the same diffuse way, and that's much harder to detect than a wrong fact.

So I'd say: real effect, probably mechanistically interesting, and I'd hold off on the stronger interpretations until the controls are in.

r001.rationale: The response suggests a possible shared truth-related feature that fine-tuning may sharpen, but does not clearly interpret the result as evidence of a pre-existing latent fact-verification capability.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s really interesting, because it suggests that something other than learning new facts is happening during fine-tuning. If the facts you’re testing are unrelated to the training sentences, then perhaps the model already had the information it needed, and the training changed how it accesses or uses that information.

But I’d be cautious about concluding that it’s learned some general notion of truth. There are a few possibilities here. Maybe it’s getting better at distinguishing things it knows from things it doesn’t. Maybe it’s learning a decision rule that happens to transfer. Or maybe there are shared features of the training and test sentences that make the task easier without improving factual reasoning more broadly.

What I’d want to see is how far that transfer goes. Does it hold across different topics and different ways of asking the question? And what happens if you fine-tune on false sentences instead? Those comparisons would help distinguish a change in how the model uses its knowledge from a change in what kinds of answers it tends to give.

r001.rationale: The response suggests the model may already have had the needed information, but does not clearly interpret the result as evidence of a pre-existing fact-verification capability. It instead offers several possible explanations and cautions against concluding that the model learned a general notion of truth.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really interesting result, because it suggests that some of what the model learns during fine-tuning transfers beyond the particular facts you’re showing it. If you train on true sentences about one topic and get better at verifying facts about another, then memorizing those training sentences can’t be the whole explanation.

One possibility is that the model already has information relevant to those other facts, and fine-tuning changes how it uses that information. You might be making it more likely to draw on something it already knows, or changing what kinds of evidence it treats as reliable.

But I’d be careful about jumping from that result to saying the model has learned some general notion of truth. I’d want to know what happens with false sentences, how unrelated the topics really are, and whether the improvement survives changes in how you ask the verification question. Those comparisons would help distinguish a change in factual reasoning from a change in confidence or response behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says the model may already contain relevant information and fine-tuning may change how it uses that information. It does not clearly interpret the result as evidence of a pre-existing fact-verification capability.
